question_en: A construction firm reports financial results under US GAAP. In 20X8, the firm borrowed $10 million for five years at 6% interest to construct its new headquarters building, which will have a useful life of 50 years and will be depreciated using the straight-line method. Construction will take three years to complete, and during that period the firm will earn $40,000 interest per year by temporarily investing the loan proceeds that it does not currently require for construction. If the firm has no other long-term assets and the loan requires only interest to be paid each year (ie, no amortization of principal), the amount of interest that the firm will capitalize is closest to:
explanation_en:
Capitalized interest arises when a firm borrows to create a long-term asset (eg, a factory). The interest expense from the loan is added to the
cost of the asset and increases the carrying value of the asset on the balance sheet. Instead of being included as interest expense, the
capitalized interest increases depreciation expense each year.
The firm incurs interest expense of $600,000 ($10 million × 6%) per year on the loan. Both IFRS and GAAP specify that interest is capitalized
during the construction period only. Interest is treated as a cost of acquisition. When the construction is finished, the asset has been "acquired"
and requires no further acquisition expenditures. The firm's construction lasts three years, so the total capitalized interest is $1.80 million.
IFRS and US GAAP treat capitalized interest similarly; the main difference concerns income received from temporarily investing loan proceeds
during construction. IFRS require firms to offset the amount of capitalized interest by the income, but GAAP do not allow this. The firm reports
under US GAAP, so it cannot offset the $120,000 income received ($40,000 per year for three years) against the $1.80 million capitalized interest
(Choice A).
(Choice C) The firm will treat the final two years of interest costs as ordinary interest expenses on the income statement. $3 million results from
capitalizing interest for the entire five-year loan period.

question_en: A company acquires the assets of another company in a business combination and records goodwill. Under US GAAP, which of the following is most likely included in goodwill?
option_b: The fair market value of PPE
explanation_en:
In a business combination, the difference between the purchase price and fair market value of net assets (ie, assets − liabilities) is goodwill. At
the time of the merger, long-lived tangible assets and identifiable intangibles are not reported as goodwill; instead, they are revalued to their fair
market value. Intangible assets are identifiable and are included in the fair market value of net assets if:
Under US GAAP, they:
Originate as a legal claim (eg, patents, trademarks)
Are separable (ie, can be sold separately) from the acquired company
Under IFRS, they:
Originate as a legal claim (eg, patents, trademarks)
Are separable (ie, can be sold separately) from the acquired company
Are controlled by the acquiring company
Can create measurable economic benefits
Have reliably measured costs
If intangible assets do not meet these criteria, they are not included in the fair market value of net assets and are accounted for as goodwill.
(Choice A) Under US GAAP, if an intangible asset originates as a legal claim or is separable (eg, a patent), it is considered an identifiable
intangible asset and is not included in goodwill.
(Choice B) Tangible assets are revalued to their fair market value in a business combination. By definition, a tangible asset's (eg, PPE's) fair
market value is identifiable and is not part of goodwill.

question_en: Under US GAAP, an impairment of property, plant, and equipment (PPE) most likely occurs when the carrying amount is:
option_a: more than the sum of the asset's discounted future cash flows.
option_b: less than the sum of the asset's undiscounted future cash flows.
option_c: more than the sum of the asset's undiscounted future cash flows.
explanation_en:
Impairment typically arises from an unanticipated decline in an asset's value. An asset is impaired when its carrying amount (ie, its book value)
is greater than its recoverable amount. Under US GAAP, the recoverable amount is measured as the sum of the asset's undiscounted future
cash flows, which represents total future economic benefits. Simply stated, an asset is impaired if its expected future benefits are below its current
book value.
When impairment occurs, the value of the asset is reduced on the balance sheet and an impairment charge is simultaneously reported on the
income statement. According to US GAAP, impairment charges may never be reversed, even if the asset's value increases in the future.
(Choices A and B) Under US GAAP, impairment occurs when the carrying value is more than the sum of the undiscounted future cash flows.

question_en: At the beginning of 20X2, a company reporting under US GAAP purchases a patent for USD 20 million with no residual value and a useful life of 10 years. At the end of 20X3, the company determines that the patent's expected cash generation is lower due to changes in the law. It estimates the following: If the company uses straight-line amortization, the 20X3 impairment charge the company records is closest to:
explanation_en:
Impairment is recognized when an asset's carrying value (ie, historical cost less accumulated amortization) is greater than its undiscounted
future cash flows (ie, recoverable amount). The actual impairment loss is the difference between the asset's carrying value and its fair
market value.
In this scenario, determine the carrying value at the end of 20X3. Using the straight-line method, the amortization expense is USD 2 million per
year. The carrying value at the end of 20X3 is found by subtracting two years (20X2 and 20X3) of amortization from its historical cost.
Since the carrying value is greater than the undiscounted cash flow, the company records an impairment loss. The amount of the loss (USD 7
million) is the difference between the carrying value (USD 16 million) and the fair market value (USD 9 million).
(Choice A) USD 6 million is found by using the undiscounted future cash flow, not the fair market value when calculating the impairment charge.
(Choice C) USD 8 million is found by subtracting the net fair market value from the asset's carrying value since that is greater than its value in
use. Under IFRS, the recoverable amount is the greater of the fair market value net of selling costs or its value in use.

question_en:
A company reports under US GAAP and provides the following information on its equipment:

| Metric | $ |
|---|---|
| Carrying amount | 31,000 |
| Expected future cash flows: Undiscounted | 28,000 |
| Expected future cash flows: Present value | 26,500 |
| Fair value if sold | 22,000 |
| Cost to sell | 2,500 |

Due to an impairment charge, the carrying value of the machine is closest to:
explanation_en:
Impairment charges are recognized when an asset's carrying amount, measured as historical cost minus accumulated depreciation, is greater
than its recoverable value. US GAAP defines the recoverable amount as simply the undiscounted expected future cash flows. In this case,
the carrying amount ($31,000) exceeds the recoverable amount ($28,000).
The impaired asset is written down to a new carrying value with a new depreciation schedule. Under US GAAP, the asset would be written down
to fair value (ie, value if sold [$22,000]). This fair value estimate becomes the new carrying amount.
In contrast, IFRS defines the recoverable amount and the new carrying value as the greater of the asset's fair value less costs to sell the asset
($22,000 − $2,500) or the discounted future cash flows ($26,500) that the asset is expected to generate (Choices A and C).

question_en: In 20X7, a firm reported earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of €32.2 million, interest expense of €3.5 million on its income statement, and interest paid of €3.1 million on its cash flow statement. The footnotes also revealed that if the firm had no capitalized interest in 20X7, depreciation expense would change by €450,000. After factoring in all effects of capitalized interest, the analyst recalculated the interest coverage ratio to be 7.5 times. The amount of capitalized interest reported by the firm in 20X7 is closest to:
explanation_en:
Firms that report capitalized interest usually have an overstated interest coverage ratio. Capitalized interest is included with noncurrent (ie,
long-term) assets and not as an expense on the income statement, so interest expense is less for firms that capitalize, resulting in a larger ratio.
The firm pays the interest each year, so from an analytical perspective, it is irrelevant whether the firm records the interest as an expense or an
asset. Analysts routinely adjust the interest coverage ratio to add the capitalized interest to the interest paid.
Another adjustment must be made for depreciation. When a noncurrent asset includes capitalized interest, it is expenses as incrementally higher
depreciation expense. For example, if a noncurrent asset includes $100 of capitalized interest, and the asset is depreciated straight-line over ten
years, then depreciation expense increases by $10 each year (= 100/10). This additional depreciation is added to earnings before interest and
taxes (EBIT).
So, the total adjustment requires two steps:
adjust for the capitalized interest (in the denominator) to reflect the firm's "true" interest cost.
adjust for additional depreciation expense (in the numerator).
The adjustments to the firm's interest coverage ratio are shown below:
(Choice A) 850,000 results from incorrectly using interest expense rather than interest paid in the interest coverage ratio.
(Choice B) 1,133,333 results from an incorrect numerator caused by subtracting the incremental depreciation from EBIT instead of adding it to
EBIT.

question_en: A company acquires an asset that has a cost of ¥90 million, a useful life of 3 years, and zero salvage value. The asset will be abandoned at the end of 3 years. The company does not pay dividends. All else being equal, expensing the cost of this asset, instead of capitalizing it, will most likely result in:
option_a: higher return on equity at the end of the first year.
option_b: lower cash from investing activities in the first year.
option_c: the same retained earnings at the end of the asset's useful life.
explanation_en:
Expensing an asset captures its full cost on the income statement when the asset is purchased. In contrast, capitalizing an asset initially captures
its full cost as a long-term asset on the balance sheet and subsequently spreads its depreciation expense to the income statement over the asset's
useful life.
Due to this timing difference, expensing results in lower net income initially and higher net income in subsequent years. In contrast, net income
is more even each year during the asset's useful life when its cost is capitalized. However, the total net income over the asset's life is the same
under both methods. Since retained earnings are the accumulation of net income, net of any dividends paid (which in this case is zero), retained
earnings at the end of the asset's life are identical whether the asset is capitalized or expensed.
For example, assume this company begins operations in Year 0 with ¥200 million in cash and purchases the asset in Year 1. Furthermore,
assume the asset generates annual revenue of ¥100 million, as shown:
If expensed, the full ¥90 million cost is captured as net income in Year 1. If capitalized, the ¥90 million appears on the balance sheet under Gross
PPE in Year 1 and subsequently reduces each year's income by ¥30 million (before tax) in depreciation (assuming the straight-line method is
used). At the end of 3 years, retained earnings under both scenarios equal ¥168 million.
(Choice A) Expensing (compared to capitalizing) an asset results in lower ROE (= net income / average shareholders' equity) during the first year
since Year 1's net income is proportionally reduced more than average shareholders' equity.
(Choice B) Expensing an asset results in greater cash flow from investing activities since the full cost, which is a negative cash flow, is reflected
in cash from operating activities.

question_en: At the beginning of this year, a company purchased electronic goods that cost €120,000 and chose to expense the purchase instead of capitalizing it. The electronics have a useful life of 3 years with zero salvage value, and the company uses straight-line depreciation. The company reports €300,000 in revenue each year and is taxed at 25%. There are no other expenses aside from the purchase cost and corporate tax. Based only on this information and compared to capitalizing the asset, expensing the asset most likely results in:
option_a: net PPE that is €120,000 lower in the current year.
option_b: net income that is €60,000 lower in the current year.
option_c: cash from operations that is €100,000 higher in the current year.
explanation_en:
Expensing or capitalizing an asset purchase impacts the company's financial results differently each year, but the cumulative impact to net income
and total cash flow under both methods is the same over time. In this scenario, when the company expenses the asset, the full cost of €120,000
is reported on the income statement this year. Subtracting €120,000 from revenue of €300,000 results in pretax income of €180,000, which yields
€135,000 of net income after deducting €45,000 of taxes.
Had the company capitalized the asset, at initial recognition €120,000 would be reported on the balance sheet as a long-term asset. At year-end,
€40,000 of depreciation (ie, €120,000 purchase price less 0 salvage value over 3 years) is reported as depreciation expense on the income
statement and reduces pretax income to €260,000, which yields €195,000 in net income after subtracting €65,000 in taxes. Therefore, expensing
the asset would result in net income that is 135,000 − 195,000 = €60,000 lower in the first year.

question_en: A company purchased equipment at the beginning of 20X2. At the end of 20X2, the fair value of the equipment fell to €10,000 below its book value. Using the revaluation model and ignoring tax effects, on the 20X2 financial reports, this most likely results in a €10,000 reduction in:
explanation_en:
Financial statement treatment of revaluation of noncurrent assets—IFRS only
Upward revaluation Downward revaluation
Gain recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) as
Initial Loss recognized on income statement
revaluation surplus
Recognized on income statement to the extent of previous
Reduces revaluation surplus
recognized losses
Subsequent If revaluation surplus = 0, recognized on income
Gain in excess of previous losses recognized as revaluation
statement as loss

Companies that report under IFRS are permitted to revalue long-term assets to their current fair value. An upward revaluation occurs when an
asset's fair value exceeds its carrying amount (ie, net book value). A downward revaluation occurs when an asset's fair value falls below its
carrying amount.
The accounting treatment for each case is:
For an initial upward revaluation, the initial gain from the asset mark-up bypasses the income statement and directly increases other
comprehensive income, reported as a component of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.
For an initial downward adjustment, the initial loss from the asset mark-down appears on the income statement and reduces net income,
which then flows to shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.
The different treatments of the upward and downward revaluations reflect accounting standards' conservative bias: the company must "own" the
downward revaluation and report it as directly affecting net income, and thus earnings performance, but cannot similarly "take credit" for an
upward revaluation.
In this scenario, the fair value of the asset drops below its balance sheet book value, so a downward revaluation occurs. This directly reduces net
income by €10,000.
(Choice B) Since the downward revaluation occurs at the end of 20X2, the depreciation expense will be adjusted going forward. Therefore, there
is no change to accumulated depreciation in 20X2.
(Choice C) Only upward revaluations impact other comprehensive income on the balance sheet.

explanation_en:
A gain or loss from the sale of a noncurrent asset is reported on the income statement. The gain or loss is calculated as the difference between
the sales price and the asset's book value at the time of sale. As the figure above demonstrates, book value is the difference between the
historical cost of the asset and the asset's accumulated depreciation.
Inserting the variables for book value into the equation for gain or loss on sale results in the relationship on the right in the figure. All variables to
calculate the gain or loss are known except for the accumulated depreciation.
Rearranging the equation on the right results in:
(Choice B) $1,000,000 is the difference between the sales price and the historical cost. It does not account for any depreciation that would
reduce the historical cost to the current book value.
(Choice C) $1,900,000 results from mistaking the $900,000 loss as a gain and adding it to the difference between the historic cost and the sales

question_en: A company reporting under IFRS elects to use the revaluation model for its equipment. The company purchases equipment for €10 million during 20X3. At the end of 20X3, the fair value of the equipment is €11 million. The company most likely records a €1 million:
explanation_en:
Financial statement treatment of revaluation of noncurrent assets—IFRS only
Upward revaluation Downward revaluation
Gain recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) as
Initial Loss recognized on income statement
revaluation surplus
Recognized on income statement to the extent of previous
Reduces revaluation surplus
recognized losses
Subsequent If revaluation surplus = 0, recognized on income
Gain in excess of previous losses recognized as revaluation
statement as loss

IFRS, but not US GAAP, allow companies to choose between the cost model and the revaluation model for valuing long-lived assets. Using the
revaluation model, an asset's carrying value is adjusted based on the asset's fair value. Revaluations adjust an asset's carrying value upward
or downward. These adjustments may be made during the initial year of ownership and/or subsequently over the equipment's useful life.
An initial upward revaluation means that the company reports the asset at a higher value than its original cost. For an initial upward revaluation,
the increase in value bypasses the income statement and is reported as part of other comprehensive income; it is not recorded as a gain and
has no impact on expenses or net income (Choices B and C). The revaluation bypasses the income statement since the higher valuation is
outside of management's control and so the company should not report increased profits from it.
The company may record an increase in profits only if there is a subsequent increase in fair value following previous reductions in value. Then the
increase in fair value—and profit—is limited to previous decreases in value. Any increase in value above previous losses is also recorded in other
comprehensive income.

question_en: A decision to capitalize the purchase of a long-lived asset instead of expensing it will most likely result in a company reporting:
option_a: less net income in the first year.
option_b: greater cash flow from investing activities in the first year.
option_c: greater cash flow from operating activities in the first year.
explanation_en:
Each method of recording an asset purchase (ie, capitalizing or expensing) initially impacts the company's reported financial results differently, but
the cumulative impact under either method is the same over the course of time. A comparison of capitalization versus expensing is shown:
When a buyer capitalizes an expenditure, long-term assets increase by the amount capitalized on the balance sheet; that amount will then be
depreciated over the asset's useful life. Since the initial expenditure bypasses the income statement, net income will be greater initially compared
with expensing an asset, but will be less in future periods due to depreciation. Furthermore, capitalizing produces greater cash from operating
activities since the initial cash expenditure is classified as a cash outflow under investing activities (Choice B).
When a company expenses an asset, the initial expenditure appears as an operating expense on the income statement, which produces a lower
net income initially and less cash from operating activities compared with capitalizing the asset (Choice A). However, since no long-term asset is
recognized on the balance sheet, there is no periodic depreciation, which leads to higher net income in future periods.

question_en: Company A purchases a patent from Company B and acquires Company C along with its customer list. The most appropriate way for Company A to account for these purchases would be to:
option_a: capitalize both the patent and the customer list.
option_b: capitalize the patent and expense the customer list.
option_c: expense the patent and capitalize the customer list.
explanation_en:
Treatment for intangible assets
Acquisition method Treatment of costs
Purchased on a stand-alone basis Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet
Research costs expensed immediately on income statement
Developed internally through research
Development costs capitalized on balance sheet if product is developed for internal use (US
and development
GAAP) or has demonstrated technical feasibility (IFRS)
Acquired through a business Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet
combination (eg, merger) Additional goodwill created on balance sheet
Intangible assets (eg, patents, customer lists) lack physical form but are still expected to grant the holder future economic benefit. These assets
can be obtained through a stand-alone purchase, the acquisition of another company, or internal development.
Companies are required to account for these assets in different ways, depending on the means of acquisition. If intangible assets are acquired
through a stand-alone purchase or as part of a larger business combination (eg, acquisition), both IFRS and US GAAP require capitalizing
the asset: recognizing its fair value on the company's balance sheet and subsequently amortizing that value over the asset's useful life. Note that
goodwill, although considered an intangible asset, is not identifiable and therefore not amortized but rather periodically tested for impairment.
In this scenario, one company acquires a customer list as a part of its acquisition of another company and also purchases a stand-alone patent.
Under IFRS and US GAAP, both intangible assets should be capitalized (Choices B and C).

question_en: At the beginning of 20X7, a company acquires a trademark for $85 million; the trademark is considered held for use. At the end of 20X7, the company records an impairment charge of $20 million due to a pending lawsuit. In 20X8, the company receives a favorable ruling, and the trademark is fairly valued at $185 million at year end. If the company reports under US GAAP, the reported increase in the trademark's value for 20X8 is closest to:
explanation_en:
An impairment is an unanticipated decline in an asset's value. An asset is impaired when its carrying amount is greater than its recoverable
amount. Under US GAAP, the recoverable amount is the sum of the asset's undiscounted future cash flows (ie, total future economic benefit).
An asset is impaired if its expected future benefit is below its current book value.
After its initial impairment, the asset's value may increase. However, under US GAAP, if the asset is considered held for use (ie, PPE), a
reversal of the impairment is not allowed (Choices B and C). If the asset is considered held for sale, the company may record an increase in
the asset's carrying value limited to the amount of the initial impairment.
Under IFRS, there is no distinction between held for use and held for sale; all assets may increase in value after an initial impairment charge.
However, the increase is limited to the original impairment, even if the recoverable amount is greater than the asset's carrying value before the
initial impairment.

An asset is impaired when its carrying amount (book value) exceeds its recoverable amount. Under IFRS, the recoverable amount is the greater
of the fair value minus selling costs (ie, net fair value) or the sum of the asset's discounted future cash flows (value in use). An impairment loss
under IFRS equals the difference between the carrying amount and the recoverable amount. Here is an example of the impairment loss
calculation under IFRS, using the appropriate recoverable amount:
In this example, the company reduces the asset by EUR 15,000 on the balance sheet and simultaneously records an impairment loss of EUR
15,000 on the income statement. According to IFRS (unlike US GAAP), impairment charges can be reversed in the future if the recoverable
amount increases above the carrying value.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a reason for a company to lease, rather than purchase, an asset? The company does not have to:
option_a: report a lease liability on the balance sheet.
option_b: report a leased asset on the balance sheet.
option_c: risk disposing of the asset at a below-market residual value.
explanation_en: Leasing an asset gives the lessee the right to use the asset for a fixed time in exchange for periodic payments to the lessor (ie, owner of the asset). There are several motivations for a company to lease an asset instead or purchasing it. Less costly upfront: Leasing, unlike buying, typically does not require an up-front down payment. Looser restrictions: Leasing an asset circumvents the need to finance an expensive purchase with borrowed funds, which typically include strict covenants. Less asset disposal risk: The lessee does not have to worry about disposing of the assets at below-market salvage (ie, residual) values. Accounting rules require lessees to record the fair value of a lease as an asset and liability at the inception of the lease (Choices A and B).

option_a: expense equal to the average periodic lease payment.
option_b: long-term asset equal to the present value of lease payments.
option_c: long-term liability equal to the total amount of future lease payments.
explanation_en: Financial statement impact to the lessee Governing standard Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement Reduction of lease liability: CFF IFRS: all leases Asset Depreciation Interest payments: US GAAP: finance lease Liability Interest IFRS: CFF or CFO US GAAP: CFO Asset US GAAP: operating lease Single expense item Entire lease payment: CFO Liability In a lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset for a specified period. Under IFRS, all leases are treated like asset purchases financed with borrowed funds (similar to the treatment of finance leases under US GAAP). At inception, the lessee records on its balance sheet a long-term asset and liability equal to the present value of the future lease payments (Choice C). The lessee depreciates the asset during the term of the lease. The periodic lease payments are apportioned toward interest payments and liability reduction each period. In this respect, a lease is conceptually very similar to amortizing a long-term loan. (Choice A) Under US GAAP, the amount of the average periodic lease payment in an operating lease is recorded as an expense each period on the income statement. question_en: A company maintains a defined benefit plan for its employees. It recently determined that its employees' life expectancy has increased, which will increase the company's pension liability. The amount of the increased liability can only be estimated. Under US GAAP, the company most appropriately reports the increased liability on its financial statements:
option_a: in the footnotes only, since it cannot determine the amount of increase.
option_b: as part of other comprehensive income and amortizes the increase over time.
option_c: as part of other comprehensive income but does not amortize the increase over time.
explanation_en: Financial statement impact to the lessee Governing standard Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement Reduction of lease liability: CFF IFRS: all leases Asset Depreciation Interest payments: US GAAP: finance lease Liability Interest IFRS: CFF or CFO US GAAP: CFO Asset US GAAP: operating lease Single expense item Entire lease payment: CFO Liability In a lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset for a specified amount of time. Under IFRS, all leases are treated like asset purchases financed with borrowed funds. At inception, the lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability equal to the present value of the future lease payments. After inception, periodic payments are separated into two categories: A portion is applied toward reducing the lease liability principal and is recorded as a cash outflow under financing activities. The rest of the monthly payment counts as interest and is recorded as a cash outflow under financing activities or operating activities. Note that the interest portion of the lease payments is classified under financing or operating activities under IFRS but is strictly classified as operating activities under US GAAP. (Choice A) Under IFRS, the principal portion of the lease payment cannot be classified as an operating activity. (Choice B) Under IFRS, the reduction of the lease liability is treated as a cash outflow from financing, not investing.

subtopic: 5.08 Topics in Long-Term Liabilities and Equity
question_en: The impact on a lessor's financial statements in the first year of a lease that was newly classified as a sales-type lease rather than a direct-financing lease is most likely higher:
explanation_en: Long-term leases under US GAAP: lessee's perspective Type Balance sheet Income statement Cash flow statement Reduction of lease liability: Asset Depreciation Finance lease ↓ CFF Liability Interest Interest payments: ↓ CFO Asset Operating lease Single expense Entire lease payment: ↓ CFO Liability In a long-term lease contract, the lessee makes periodic payments to the lessor for the right to use an asset (ie, right of use [ROU]) for a specified period. Under US GAAP, long-term leases can be classified as finance or operating. Finance leases are treated like asset purchases financed with borrowed funds (from the lessor). At inception, the lessee simultaneously records an ROU asset and a lease liability, both equal to the present value of the future lease payments. After inception, a portion of each periodic payment is applied toward reducing the liability (ie, principal reduction), which reduces cash from financing activities. Therefore, cash flow from financing (CFF) is less under a finance lease. The rest of the monthly payment counts as interest and reduces cash from operating activities (CFO). Operating leases are treated like rental agreements. In each period, the entire periodic payment is treated like rent expense and reduces cash from operating activities on the cash flow statement. Therefore, CFO under an operating lease is less than CFO under a finance lease (Choice B). (Choice C) After inception, periodic payments do not affect cash flows from investing activities regardless of lease type.
